newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Senate overcomes IR, looks to budget.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Senate overcomes IR, looks to budget.

text.p: The Senate logjam is starting to free up now that the upper house has passed the Workplace Relations and Other Legislation Amendment Bill.
With the the new industrial relations system finally out of the way, the Senate is moving on to budget legislation.
Right now the Senate has these bills on its plate, none of them controversial:
-- The Income Tax Rates Amendment (Family Tax Initiative) Bill, which is fiscally unimportant because it proposes to spend money, not save it.
-- The three appropriations bills, the legislation granted almost automatically to finance government operations.
Those bills will probably take until early next week, by which time there will be less than three weeks' of sittings before Christmas.

So the government has to make a decision: does it immediately press ahead with the Telstra (Dilution of Public Ownership) Bill, as long planned, or does it sideline Telstra for a while and concentrate on the controversial budget bills.
Among the controversial budget bills, one is already listed for debate, the one that would extend migrants' waiting periods for social security.

There is a good chance that bill will not survive, so the government also has to decide whether to drop it for the moment and spend the precious time on achievable legislation instead. (For the record, that bill's name is the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Newly Arrived Resident's Waiting Periods and Other Measures) Bill -- quite a mouthful.)
None the less, the industrial relations legislation is finally out of the way, after a near-record 49 1/2 hours of debate. We can now expect some legislative progress.
MEANWHILE, AT GOVERNMENT HOUSE
Your correspondent believes he has detected a Monty Python plot against the U.S. president.
Bill Clinton this morning visited Australian Governor-General Sir William Deane, his motorcade flashing down the picturesque drive that leads to Government House, Deane's official residence.

Outside, at the gates of Government House, a little crowd of onlookers gathered, watched by slightly nervous police and protective agents, who made sure no cars were parked too close to the road, presumably for fear of bombs.

Suddenly a semi-trailer, labelled Joe's Plant Supplies or something, came roaring down the drive, a dead-end. The driver got to the gates and tried a U-turn, placing the semi across the road, which must have driven the protective agents crazy.
Eventually he moved it off the road and then, incongruously, got out, took a large potted shrubbery from the trailer and placed it on the grass next to the road.
He then roared off again.

Now your correspondent, not naturally paranoid, could not help thinking this was an unusual coincidence -- that someone should place a shrubbery alongside a road for no readily apparent reason shortly before the U.S. president was supposed to drive past it.
The shrubbery did not, however, explode when the motorcade whizzed past. Your correspondent noted this from behind a tree.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
